confidence_note: The special forces scene and quotes come from a published excerpt of the book and a review citing p.23. The old text's CEO conversation and invented armor names have no source and were dropped. The armored/daring pairs come from summaries of the book.
facts: In 2014 Brown stood in front of several hundred military special forces soldiers on a base in the Midwest.
She defined vulnerability as the emotion we experience during uncertainty, risk and emotional exposure.
She asked: 'Can you give me a single example of courage that you've witnessed in another soldier or experienced in your own life that did not require experiencing vulnerability?'
A young soldier said: 'No, ma'am. Three tours. I can't think of a single act of courage that doesn't require managing massive vulnerability.'
Brown has since asked the question a couple of hundred times in meeting rooms around the world.

She contrasts armored leadership (perfectionism and fear of failure, being the knower who must be right, power over people, collecting gold stars) with daring leadership (healthy striving, being a learner, power with people, giving gold stars).
Brown: 'When we get to the place that the armor is so thick that we no longer feel anything, we experience a real death.'
Brown: 'Vulnerability is not winning or losing. It's having the courage to show up when you can't control the outcome.'
scene_details: several hundred special forces soldiers on a Midwest base
collecting gold stars vs giving them
tension: A researcher tells a room of elite soldiers that courage needs vulnerability, and waits for one counterexample.
opening_idea: Open on the silence after her question in front of the soldiers.

lessons.idea: Notice the armor you put on when unsure, such as needing to be the one who knows, and replace one instance with an honest 'I'm not sure yet'.
lessons.anchor: Knower vs learner pair; the soldier's 'managing massive vulnerability'.
lessons.everyday_example_idea: A new shift manager who always answers instantly, even when guessing, versus saying she will check.

reflect_final: In which recurring conversation do you most need to look like the one who knows, and what would you say there if you dropped that need?

use_cases.situation: Your team expects you to have the answer to a new problem.
use_cases.move: Say you do not know yet, name what you will find out, and invite their ideas.

use_cases.situation: A colleague hides that a task is beyond them.
use_cases.move: Mention the soldier's three tours and that courage meant managing vulnerability, then ask what is hard for them.

use_cases.situation: Your teenager will not admit a mistake.
use_cases.move: Admit a mistake of your own first, plainly.

pocket_idea: Even soldiers after three tours could not name courage without vulnerability; drop the armor once today.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Brown asked hundreds of special forces soldiers for one act of courage without vulnerability, and nobody could give one.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: 2014 base, question, silence, soldier's three tours answer; she has asked it a couple hundred times since.
